analysis.paper_title: TRIMMED k-MEANS: AN ATTEMPT TO ROBUSTIFY QUANTIZERS
analysis.authors_year: J. A. Cuesta-Albertos, A. Gordaliza and C. Matrán (1997)
analysis.research_question: How can k-means clustering and related quantizers be robustified via impartial trimming while establishing mathematical analysis, existence, and strong consistency of the resulting trimmed k-means?
analysis.context: Clustering and quantization procedures based on k-means minimization are sensitive to outliers and extreme values. Although standard robust techniques like data removal exist, they often introduce arbitrariness in selecting zones for removal. This paper extends Gordaliza's impartial trimming methodology to robustify k-means and analyzes its theoretical and practical performance.
methods: Formulation of impartial a-trimmed k-means using generalized trimming functions and penalty functions
Theoretical proofs of existence and strong consistency using Skorohod representation and empirical measures
Simulation studies on bivariate normal mixture models contaminated by outliers and inlayers across various cluster dispersions and trimming sizes
Application of simulated annealing-based algorithms in a Matlab setting to handle optimization challenges
main_findings: Optimal trimming functions essentially coincide with indicator functions of unions of k balls with identical radii
Trimmed k-means induce a partition into k spherical clusters of equal radius where cluster centers are phi-means of their respective clusters
Strong consistency of trimmed k-means is established under continuity assumptions of the underlying probability distribution
Simulations demonstrate successful detection of anomalous observations and robust cluster estimation under high contamination proportions
assumptions: The penalty function Phi is continuous, nondecreasing, with Phi(0) = 0 and Phi(x) < Phi(infinity) for all x
The probability distribution PX of the random vector is continuous
The number of clusters k and the trimming level alpha are given
limitations_explicit: Clusters obtained by the method are spherical and share the same radius, meaning relatively nearby clusters can be badly detected if they are nonspherical or have very different shapes
There is no deterministic optimal algorithm to choose the optimal trimming set, requiring random algorithms like simulated annealing
The breakdown point of the a-trimmed k-mean depends heavily on the data and can be bounded by the probability mass of true underlying clusters

potential_open_questions.question: How can the limitation of spherical clusters of equal radius be overcome for clusters with different shapes or anisotropic dispersions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The theoretical derivation proves that optimal trimming functions correspond to balls of equal radius centered at the k cluster centers, imposing spherical geometry on the clusters.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The authors note that Corollary 3.2 implies every cluster obtained is spherical with the same radius, which can lead to poor detection if clusters are nonspherical or have different shapes.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: Note that, from Corollary 3.2, it follows that relatively nearby clusters could be badly detected if they are nonspherical or even if their shapes are too different because, according to that corollary, every cluster obtained with our method is spherical and all of them have the same radius. Therefore, the ideal model would be one consisting of spherical, not too close, clusters. Moreover, in that ideal model, the anomalous observations should appear clearly separated from the nonanomalous ones. Here we have chosen a sample of situations in which each requirement to have an ideal model is violated. Moreover, all of them have in common that many of the anomalous data are not so anomalous because the only restriction we have imposed on them is that they are not allowed to be in the 75% level confidence ellipsoids of the distributions generating the points in the clusters.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: The breakdown point of the a-trimmed k-mean depends on the data configuration and is bounded by the probability mass of the individual clusters.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Specific examples with uniform distributions on discrete sets show that contamination can force arbitrary trimming choices or severely affect location estimates depending on underlying cluster proportions.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The analysis of breakdown points and contaminated discrete examples indicates that the breakdown point of the a-trimmed k-mean is bounded by the proportions of the true underlying clusters.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: A careful look at this example shows that the cause of this behavior of the 2-mean procedure when applied to the uniform probability on A is that, if we are looking for just two clusters, then the set A already contains 1/3 of anomalous points (independently of when those points constitute or do not constitute a new cluster.). Therefore, it seems that for probabilities Q, supported by a set which is divided into exactly k clusters with respective probabilities q1, q2, ..., qk, the breakdown point of the a-trimmed k-mean of Q is, at most, inf{a, q1, ..., qk} independently of ͕. Of course, this fact is more apparent when we use other methods like the ‘two joint medians’ example in the Introduction, which is clearly unstable in every circumstance. In other words, the breakdown point generally depends, of course, on the procedure, but it also depends heavily on the data, in the sense that the same procedure can be highly stable with reasonable clusterized data when considering the right number of clusters, but it can also be very unstable in other cases.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Replacing spherical variance criteria with tailored scatter-estimation criteria (such as determinant minimization of group scatter matrices) enables proper cluster detection in highly linear or non-spherical mixtures.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Standard trimmed k-means fails on linear clusters because it assumes spherical shapes; incorporating group-specific scatter matrices resolves this limitation.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The authors demonstrate that utilizing a generalized dispersion criterion successfully uncovers structure in highly linear clusters where standard curves fail.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt:
Figure 8 (top) exhibits the trimmed k-variance functionals when k = 1 and 2 for a sample composed of 100 observations from a bivariate normal with mean vector (0, 0)' and 100 observations from another bivariate normal with mean vector (10, 0)', and both having covariance matrix

However, in Figure 8 (bottom) we see a clear “jump” at α = 0.5 when k = 1 in the curve obtained plotting the values obtained from (4.1) against α (discovering that each group accounts for 50% of the data points).

analysis.paper_title: Implementing the Fisher's Discriminant Ratio in a k-Means Clustering Algorithm for Feature Selection and Data Set Trimming
analysis.authors_year: Thy-Hou Lin, Huang-Te Li, and Keng-Chang Tsai, 2004
analysis.research_question: How can simultaneous feature selection and data set trimming using Fisher's discriminant ratio and a k-means clustering algorithm improve the statistical significance and predictive performance of 3D-QSAR regression models for HIV-1 protease inhibitors?
analysis.context: Building quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) models often suffers from background noise and outliers among compound data sets. Effective feature selection and outlier elimination are critical to enhancing model robustness and predictive statistics like q2 in drug discovery applications.
methods: Computing 43 molecular descriptors (topologic, geometric, electronic, and 3D-QSAR) scaled between 1 and 0 for 221 HIV-1 protease inhibitors divided into five classes based on pKi values.
Using Fisher's discriminant ratio combined with a stepwise correlation-incorporating procedure for feature selection.
Employing a k-means clustering algorithm with two clusters per class for each selected descriptor to identify and discard inhibitors in bad clusters as outliers.

Evaluating model quality and statistical significance using linear regression normal equations, cross-validated r2 (q2), external validation parameters, representation entropy, MREG stepwise variable selection, and SYBYL CoMFA and Cerius2 PLS regression analyses.
main_findings: Simultaneous feature selection and data set trimming using k-means clustering progressively reduced descriptor and inhibitor counts while enhancing the statistical significance of CoMFA PLS and Cerius2 PLS regression models.

The best feature selection and data set trimming results for inhibitors divided into five classes were achieved when selecting three descriptors (Hosoya Z4, Hosoya Z6, and Hosoya Z3), retaining 98 inhibitors and yielding an improved q2 of 0.727.
Most of the selected good features were topological descriptors that correlated well with measured pKi values.
Scaling descriptor values between 1 and 0 was essential because unscaled descriptors risked biasing cost functions toward larger numerical ranges.
assumptions: Descriptors can be effectively scaled to lie between 1 and 0 to remove bias from different dynamic ranges.
Compounds with descriptor values falling into the smallest-value cluster across all selected descriptors represent outliers with less class-sensitive properties that should be trimmed.
Class separability can be adequately quantified using Fisher's discriminant ratio for the data sets studied.
limitations_explicit: The proposed feature selection algorithm is not invariant under a transformation of the variables.
More complicated classification rules like the Bayesian rule require a priori knowledge about class distributions.

potential_open_questions.question: How effective are alternative clustering algorithms besides k-means when applied in combination with Fisher's discriminant ratio for feature selection and data set trimming across more structurally diverse or complex pharmaceutical data sets?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The study demonstrates that k-means works well for the specific dataset tested, but leaves open whether other clustering schemes would generalize similarly without requiring custom tuning or prior distribution knowledge.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The authors note that while k-means performs well, other classification or clustering techniques might be explored, though more complex rules might introduce additional requirements.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: While the k-means clustering scheme performs well in combination with the feature selection process, other classification techniques may be also effective in providing the trimming in the process. However, a more complicated classification rule such as the Bayesian one requires some a priori knowledge about the distribution of classes. All CoMFA experience suggests that the only action capable of changing the sign of a q2 value is realigning some or all of the molecules. Our method will be useful when all the biological data are sound and there are either no structurally obvious ways to align the molecules or those ways fail to produce a satisfactory q2.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Alternative advanced classification or partitioning techniques could replace k-means clustering to achieve comparable or superior data set trimming and feature selection performance in QSAR studies.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: The paper highlights that k-means is just one possible clustering scheme and suggests exploring other classifiers, provided they do not overly complicate classification assumptions.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The text suggests exploring other classification techniques alongside the feature selection process.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: While the k-means clustering scheme performs well in combination with the feature selection process, other classification techniques may be also effective in providing the trimming in the process. However, a more complicated classification rule such as the Bayesian one requires some a priori knowledge about the distribution of classes. All CoMFA experience suggests that the only action capable of changing the sign of a q2 value is realigning some or all of the molecules. Our method will be useful when all the biological data are sound and there are either no structurally obvious ways to align the molecules or those ways fail to produce a satisfactory q2.

analysis.research_question: What are the robustness and consistency properties of robust k-means (RKM), and how does its universal breakdown point and performance behave under general versus well-structured datasets?
analysis.context: Over recent years, various variations of the quadratic k-means clustering procedure have been proposed to robustify performance in the presence of outliers, primarily via penalized regularization methods or trimming functions. This work provides a theoretical analysis of robust k-means (RKM), a variant of classical quadratic k-means borrowing ideas from outlier detection in regression.
methods: Formulating the robust k-means problem using the Moreau envelope and proximal maps
Analyzing the finite sample breakdown point (specifically the universal breakdown point) under biased and unbiased proximal maps
Evaluating restricted robustness under the assumption of (rho_1, rho_2)-balanced well-structured datasets
Proving consistency properties using Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory and empirical process techniques
Conducting synthetic data experiments comparing RKM and trimmed k-means (TKM) across various contamination scenarios
main_findings: Two outliers in a dataset are sufficient to breakdown clustering centers when using biased proximal maps (convex penalties).
The universal breakdown point of robust k-means with an unbiased proximal map is 2/n for arbitrary datasets.
When restricted to well-structured (rho_1, rho_2)-balanced datasets, robust k-means successfully ignores the influence of outliers when grouping inliers.
Loss consistency and consistency (in probability) hold for robust k-means with a non-asymptotic rate of convergence of order O(sqrt(log n / n)).
Robust k-means and trimmed k-means perform remarkably similar in practice across synthetic clustering and contamination experiments.
assumptions: The function phi is lower semi-continuous, symmetric, with a minimum value phi(0).
The error penalty function f_lambda is symmetric, lsc, proper, and bounded from below.
For well-structured datasets, inlier samples are covered by unions of balls with bounded radius r and centers at least v apart.
limitations_explicit: Robust k-means cannot be robust against any arbitrary type of contamination and any type of dataset when relying on the universal breakdown point definition.
Unbiased proximal maps still suffer from a universal breakdown point of 2/n under general arbitrary datasets.

potential_open_questions.question: Can the universal breakdown point bounds be improved or generalized for alternative definitions of breakdown in center-based clustering with penalty-based formulations?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current tight notion of the breakdown point under arbitrary contamination yields pessimistic bounds like 2/n even for unbiased proximal maps, indicating that general contamination assumptions might be overly pessimistic.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The paper highlights that the disappointing universal breakdown result stems from the tight general definition of the breakdown point allowing any kind of contamination, suggesting that alternative or refined notions might better capture practical algorithm resilience.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: The result of Theorem 1 is disappointing but it is not (RKM) to be blamed for the poor performance but the tight notion of the definition about the breakdown point [6, 7]; allowing any kind of contamination in a dataset is a very general assumption. In this section, we place two restrictions: i) we consider datasets where inlier samples can be covered by unions of balls with centers that are “far apart” each other, and ii) we ask a question different from the finite sample breakdown point. We want to exploit as much as possible the results of [2] concerning a new quantitative measure of noise robustness which compares the output of (RKM) on a contaminated dataset to its output on the uncontaminated version of the dataset. Our aim is to show that (RKM), with a certain class of proximal maps and datasets that are well-structured ignores the influence of outliers when grouping the inliers.
sections: 3.3 Restricted robustness of robust k-means for well-clustered data

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Robust k-means (RKM) and trimmed k-means (TKM) share nearly identical statistical performance and empirical clustering behavior because both effectively eliminate or bound the influence of high-residual points despite their distinct combinatorial versus penalization formulations.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: While RKM uses a penalty regularization view via Moreau envelopes and proximal mappings while TKM uses explicit impartial trimming of top outlier points, their operational mechanisms in discarding or down-weighting extreme observations lead to matching empirical outcomes.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The author notes that despite fundamental differences between impartial trimming and penalty-based formulations, experiments confirm they share matching statistics and breakdown properties.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: As the effectiveness of robust k-means on real world and synthetic data has already been evaluated [5, 24], the purpose of this section is to relate (RKM) to trimmed k-means (TKM) [7]. Trimmed k-means is based on the methodology of “impartial trimming”, which is a combinatorial problem fundamentally different from (RKM). Despite their differences, the experiments show that, both (RKM) and (TKM) perform remarkably similar in practice. The solution of (TKM) (which is also a set of k centers) is the solution of quadratic k-means on the subsample containing ⌈n(1 − α)⌉ points with the smallest mean deviation (0 < α < 1). The only common characteristic of (RKM) and (TKM) is that they both have the same universal breakdown point, i.e., 2/n, for arbitrary datasets.

analysis.paper_title: K-means-sharp: modified centroid update for outlier-robust k-means clustering
analysis.authors_year: Peter O. Olukanmi and Bhekisipho Twala, 2017
analysis.research_question: How can the classical k-means algorithm be modified to automatically detect and avoid outliers during the clustering process without requiring user intervention or prior knowledge of the number of outliers, while preserving k-means' basic structure, simplicity, and efficiency?
analysis.context: Real-world datasets commonly contain noise and outliers, but traditional machine learning algorithms such as the classical k-means clustering algorithm assume the absence of outliers and are easily misled by them. Classical k-means computes new centroids as the mean of all data points within each cluster, meaning outliers skew cluster regionalization by contributing false large values to the objective function. Existing outlier handling techniques typically rely on separate preprocessing or post-processing modules, user-supplied parameters, or complex graph constructions that increase computational cost and violate simplicity.
methods: Modifying only the centroid update step in the classical k-means algorithm to detect and exempt putative outliers from centroid computation.
Deriving a global outlier detection threshold T from the distribution of point-to-centroid distances based on the assumption of a Gaussian data distribution.

Using the median absolute deviation (MAD_e) to compute an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation where sigma = 1.4826 MAD_e, setting the distance threshold T to 3 sigma or 4.4478 MAD_e.
Formulating a new generalized cost function that excludes outliers from the partitioning so they do not contribute to the mean squared error minimized by k-means.

Evaluating the algorithm on 10 datasets consisting of 2 standard datasets (Iris and Ruspini) and 4 outlier-contaminated versions of each dataset created by adding gross errors to 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% of the points over 100 runs.
main_findings: Given identical initializations, the proposed k-means# algorithm yields lower average error than classical k-means across all 10 tested datasets.
The outlier detection mechanism achieves an overall mean accuracy of 90.4% and precision of 86.8%, with moderate overall mean recall of 52.4% and F1-score of 61.1%.
The method requires no user intervention or prior knowledge of the number of outliers, performing clustering and outlier detection simultaneously within a single iterative structure.
assumptions: The classical k-means algorithm is an instance of the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and therefore assumes a Gaussian data distribution.
Nearly all inliers (precisely 99.73%) have point-to-centroid distances within 3 standard deviations from the population mean.
The median absolute deviation (MAD_e) provides an unbiased estimate of the population standard deviation.
limitations_explicit: The algorithm inherits the classical k-means sensitivity to initial centroid selection, meaning bad random initializations (such as when all initial centroids are outliers) can occasionally result in zero true positives.
The within-cluster error is no longer monotonically decreasing because the set of relevant inlier data changes in every iteration.

potential_open_questions.question: What is the sensitivity of the algorithm's performance metrics to varying the choice of the number of standard deviations used for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The authors fixed the boundary at 3 standard deviations based on normal distribution theory but left the systematic evaluation of varying this multiplier for future investigation.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The authors propose investigating how different multiplier values for standard deviations impact performance metrics as a direction for future work.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: A worthwhile direction for future work will be to investigate the sensitivity of the algorithm (in terms of each performance metric discussed) to the choice of the number of standard deviations for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold. Furthermore, the use of cluster-specific thresholds in contrast to a single global threshold, may improve performance, and is therefore worth exploring, although this will introduce some increase in computational cost. Lastly, since k-means# preserves the original k-means structure, it can easily benefit from many existing k-means improvements designed to address other drawbacks. Incorporation of some of these should yield increased robustness.

potential_open_questions.question: Would employing cluster-specific thresholds instead of a single global threshold improve clustering and outlier detection performance despite the increased computational cost?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current implementation relies on a single global threshold T applied across all clusters for simplicity and efficiency, leaving the performance trade-offs of cluster-specific thresholds unexplored.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The paper notes that adopting cluster-specific thresholds might enhance performance but acknowledges it would increase computational complexity.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: A worthwhile direction for future work will be to investigate the sensitivity of the algorithm (in terms of each performance metric discussed) to the choice of the number of standard deviations for determining the inlier-outlier distinction threshold. Furthermore, the use of cluster-specific thresholds in contrast to a single global threshold, may improve performance, and is therefore worth exploring, although this will introduce some increase in computational cost. Lastly, since k-means# preserves the original k-means structure, it can easily benefit from many existing k-means improvements designed to address other drawbacks. Incorporation of some of these should yield increased robustness.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Integrating special seeding techniques or advanced initialization methods into k-means# will eliminate rare cases of zero true positives caused by poor initial centroid selection.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Since k-means# inherits initialization sensitivity from classical k-means, bad initializations like selecting outliers as initial centroids lead to suboptimal performance runs.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The authors observe that bad initializations cause rare zero true positive outcomes and suggest that incorporating special seeding methods can resolve this issue.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: We note that there were rare cases among the 100 runs for some of the datasets in which k-means# returned zero true positives. Zero true positive implies undefined precision and F1 score. The problem could be caused by a bad set of randomly selected initial centroids, such as when all initial centroids are outliers. This drawback is inherited from k-means, and already mentioned in Section I. It can be addressed by incorporating special seeding methods into the algorithm, such as those discussed in Section III. Since such cases are rare in our experiments, we simply treat them as missing data and exclude them in the computation of the average values reported in Table 2. Excluding these rare cases poses no significant threat to statistical validity because reliable averages can be calculated from much less number of runs than 100.

analysis.paper_title: Sensitivity analysis of an outlier-aware k-means clustering algorithm
analysis.authors_year: Peter O. Olukanmi and Bhekisipho Twala, 2017
analysis.research_question: What is the optimal value of the constant coefficient q in determining the distance threshold T for the outlier-aware k-means clustering algorithm (k-means#), and how does varying q affect performance trade-offs in clustering quality, outlier detection accuracy, precision, and recall?
analysis.context: The study evaluates k-means# (an outlier-robust variant of classical k-means that excludes points further than a threshold T from cluster centroids during updates) under varying values of the constant coefficient q (ranging from 2 to 6, corresponding to confidence levels between 95% and near 100%). The experiments are conducted on 10 datasets, including Iris, Ruspini, and outlier-contaminated versions of each.
methods: Experimental evaluation across 10 datasets (Iris, Ruspini, and outlier-contaminated versions)
Testing performance over 100 runs per dataset for q values of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6
Measuring within-cluster mean squared error to assess clustering quality
Measuring outlier detection accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score
Analysis of variance (ANOVA) to test for differences among all k-means# versions
Paired sample t-tests for pairwise comparisons between classical k-means and each k-means# version
main_findings: For all values of q studied, k-means# yielded lower mean within-cluster squared error than classical k-means, and the difference is statistically significant.
Setting q = 2 yields the best (lowest) within-cluster mean squared error and best recall.
Setting q = 3 yields the highest overall average outlier detection accuracy (90.0%).
Precision increases as q increases, making the algorithm practically 100% precise at q > 4.
Recall and F1-score decrease as q increases, with peaks at q = 2.
assumptions: Classical k-means and the evaluated outlier-aware variant assume a Gaussian data distribution.
Points farther than threshold T from their cluster centroid are considered outliers during the centroid update step.
limitations_explicit: Comparison with classical k-means is not the primary aim of the paper.

potential_open_questions.question: What are the exact performance trade-offs and optimal parameter configurations when scaling k-means# to high-dimensional datasets with complex, non-Gaussian distributions?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current evaluation is restricted to two low-dimensional datasets (Iris and Ruspini) and their synthetic contaminated versions under the assumption of a Gaussian data distribution, leaving the algorithm's behavior on large-scale, high-dimensional, and non-Gaussian real-world data unexplored.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The authors restrict their empirical analysis to 10 datasets derived from only two base datasets (Iris and Ruspini) and explicitly operate under the Gaussian distribution assumption, meaning the generalizability of these specific q-value trade-offs to broader data domains remains an open question.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: In this paper, we investigate the effects of varying the constant coefficient q of the population standard deviation (q = 3 in the original implementation) used in computing T. We hypothesize that this value affects performance and determines the trade-offs in clustering accuracy, outlier-detection accuracy, precision and recall. This implies that varying q is expected to reduce performance along some of these dimensions while increasing others. But how sensitive is the algorithm to such variation, and is any interesting trend observable? Specifically, what is the optimal value of q when emphasis is on any one of these performance measures? To answer these questions, we study the algorithms performance on 10 datasets. The set consists of 2 popular datasets (Iris and Ruspini) and 4 outlier-contaminated versions of each. We compare average performances over 100 runs on each dataset, for q = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. These q values correspond to confidence levels between 95% and 100%. Although comparison with classical k-means is not the primary aim of this paper, k-means is included in our experiment to benchmark the clustering qualities produced by the different versions of k-means#.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Varying the constant coefficient q in the distance threshold formula affects performance and determines the trade-offs in clustering accuracy, outlier-detection accuracy, precision, and recall, resulting in improved performance along certain dimensions at the expense of others.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Because the threshold T directly governs which points are excluded as outliers during centroid updates, altering q scales the strictness of outlier rejection, directly trading off false positives (precision) against false negatives (recall).
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The paper posits and subsequently confirms through experiments that modifying the multiplier q shifts the balance between outlier detection precision, recall, and within-cluster error.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: In this paper, we investigate the effects of varying the constant coefficient q of the population standard deviation (q = 3 in the original implementation) used in computing T. We hypothesize that this value affects performance and determines the trade-offs in clustering accuracy, outlier-detection accuracy, precision and recall. This implies that varying q is expected to reduce performance along some of these dimensions while increasing others. But how sensitive is the algorithm to such variation, and is any interesting trend observable? Specifically, what is the optimal value of q when emphasis is on any one of these performance measures? To answer these questions, we study the algorithms performance on 10 datasets. The set consists of 2 popular datasets (Iris and Ruspini) and 4 outlier-contaminated versions of each. We compare average performances over 100 runs on each dataset, for q = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. These q values correspond to confidence levels between 95% and 100%. Although comparison with classical k-means is not the primary aim of this paper, k-means is included in our experiment to benchmark the clustering qualities produced by the different versions of k-means#.

analysis.research_question: How to adapt several simple and classical sampling-based k-means algorithms to the setting with outliers while achieving substantially stronger theoretical guarantees than prior work, specifically outputting at most (1 + ε)z outliers while maintaining an O(1/ε)- or O(1)-approximation to the objective function?
analysis.context: Clustering via the k-means formulation is fundamental in machine learning and data analysis, but standard k-means is highly sensitive to outliers. The k-means with outliers problem seeks a set of k cluster centers and z outliers to optimize the cost of inliers, but existing constant-factor approximation algorithms have large polynomial complexity or require outputting an unnecessarily large number of outliers (e.g., Az for a large constant A or O(log(k)·z) outliers).
methods: Reduction of k-means with outliers to k-means with (uniform) penalties via Lagrangian relaxation
Sequential sampling-based algorithms using local search (Local-search++)
Distributed coordinator-model algorithms via overseeding and weighted instance aggregation
Speeding up sampling steps using the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm
Sublinear random sampling estimators and coreset-style weighted reductions
main_findings: A sequential sampling-based algorithm (Local-search++) running in O˜(nk/ε) time that achieves an O(1/ε)-approximation while declaring at most (1 + ε)z points as outliers.
Distributed algorithms in the coordinator model where each machine sends O˜(k/ε) bits, achieving an O(1)-approximation while outputting (1 + ε)z outliers in polynomial local time.

A fast sequential algorithm running in time O˜(nk2/z) that achieves an O(1)-approximation while discarding O(z) outliers, complemented by a matching lower bound of Ω(nk2/z) in the general metric space query model.
Experimental evaluation showing that penalized and local search variants outperform baseline k-means++ and Lloyd heuristics on real-world datasets like kdd and spam.
assumptions: The minimum distance between any two points in the dataset X is lower bounded by 1.
The maximum distance between any two points Δ is bounded by poly(n).
A unit cost is assumed to evaluate the distance between two points in general metric spaces.
limitations_explicit: The sequential algorithm requires oversampling the number of centers by a factor of O(1/ε) to attain the (O(1/ε), 1 + ε)-approximation.

The deterministic lower bound proof indicates that algorithms operating in the general metric space query model that only output centers without full explicit point assignments require Ω(nk2/z) queries.

potential_open_questions.question: Can the running time of the O(1)-approximation algorithm be further improved or refined for small values of z relative to k and n using alternative coreset constructions without incurring polynomial bottlenecks?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: While current bounds match oracle-model lower bounds for center-only output algorithms, sublinear reduction of large cluster representations to k centers in general metric spaces remains complex.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Discussion regarding open challenges in reducing O(nk/z) cluster centers to k centers in sublinear time without explicit weight precomputations.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: To reduce the number of cluster centers from O(k) to k in sublinear time, we use additional sampling ideas to obtain a weighted instance that we can efficiently solve with our fast sequential algorithm. Independent of our work, (DKP20) devised an algorithm that obtains a set of O(nk/z) cluster centers that match the guarantee of our O(k) cluster centers. A slight variation of their algorithm can be implemented with running time O(nk/z), faster than our O˜(nk2/z) runtime. However, it is not clear how to reduce the O(nk/z) cluster centers to just k in sublinear time, as one cannot simply run our fast sequential algorithm on the subsampled set of cluster centers, but one additionally needs to define appropriate weights. Unlike in our case with O(k) cluster centers, it is not clear how one can define appropriate weights for the O(nk/z) cluster centers in time O˜(nk2/z).

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Refining the proofs using local search and distributed structures can yield an (O(1/poly(ε)), 1 + ε)-approximation algorithm with running time O˜(nk2/(z·poly(ε))).
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: The authors state a belief that polynomial dependencies on ε in both approximation and running time can be optimized via tighter bounds on penalty thresholds and local search iterations.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: Authors' explicit remark on potential improvements combining Appendices C and F.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: We believe, but do not prove, that refining the above proofs and using the results from Appendices C and F, we can refine Theorem 5 to achieve an (O(1/poly(ε)), 1 + ε)-approximation algorithm with running time O˜(nk2/(zpoly(ε))).

analysis.authors_year: Olga Dorabiala, J. Nathan Kutz, Aleksandr Y. Aravkin, 2022
analysis.research_question: How can we develop a robust extension of the k-means algorithm that simultaneously identifies outliers and clusters points while performing competitively on both single- and multi-membership data?
analysis.context: Clustering is fundamental in unsupervised learning, but traditional algorithms like k-means are compromised by a lack of clear separation between groups, noisy observations, and outlying data points. Existing methods that robustify k-means are typically specialized for either single- or multi-membership data and fail to perform competitively in both cases.
methods: Formulating a relaxed k-means objective where the weight matrix exists on a continuum in the capped simplex
Extending the relaxation to outlier detection by incorporating an outlier identification vector within a capped simplex without defining an explicit measure of outlierness
Solving the optimization problem using alternating minimization with Gauss-Seidel updates for centers and Proximal Alternating Minimization (PAM) for weights and outliers

Evaluating performance on single-membership datasets with outliers (WBC, shuttle training data) and multi-membership datasets with and without outliers (yeast, scene, emotions) using average F1 and Me scores
Conducting nonparametric statistical validation via Friedman and Nemenyi tests
main_findings: Robust Trimmed k-means (RTKM) successfully performs simultaneous point classification and outlier detection across both single- and multi-membership data.

On single-membership data with outliers, RTKM performs competitively with KMOR, though both RTKM and NEO-k-means trade higher outlier detection capability for increased false positives and lower F1 scores at higher outlier proportions compared to KMOR.
On multi-membership data without outliers, RTKM achieves competitive second-highest F1 scores on yeast and scene datasets and the highest on emotions compared to other multi-membership algorithms.
On multi-membership data containing outliers, RTKM consistently achieves the highest average F1 scores and achieves the lowest average Me scores under alternative noise models.
Statistical validation shows that RTKM significantly outperforms NEO-k-means in outlier identification, while holding the lowest average ranking across both F1 and Me scores.
assumptions: The expected percentage of outliers alpha and the minimum cluster membership parameter s are known or specified as inputs.
Step size parameters in the optimization updates satisfy ek > 1 and dk > 1 to guarantee convergence.
limitations_explicit: Currently, there is no principled approach to estimating the parameters alpha (proportion of expected outliers) and s (minimum cluster membership).

potential_open_questions.question: How can the objective function of RTKM be integrated into existing parameter estimation techniques (such as those used in X-means or G-means) to automatically estimate the number of clusters k?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Methods like X-means and G-means address cluster number estimation for standard k-means by running it repeatedly, but adapting these iterative criteria specifically to use the novel RTKM objective function remains an open area for future work.
potential_open_questions.evidence: Methods such as X-means [35] and G-means [36] have addressed the problem of estimating the number of clusters by running k-means repeatedly with different values of k until some criteria is satisfied. Future work could address how these methods could be altered to use our objective function to estimate k.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: We propose Robust Trimmed k-means (RTKM) as an algorithm for simultaneous point classification and outlier detection that can operate on both single- and multi-membership data. analysis.paper_title: An adaptive outlier removal aided k-means clustering algorithm
analysis.authors_year: Nawaf H.M.M. Shrifan, Muhammad F. Akbar, Nor Ashidi Mat Isa, 2022
analysis.research_question: How can the clustering accuracy and centroid convergence of the k-means algorithm be improved by combining an adapted Tukey's rule for outlier mitigation with a new angle- and RMSE-based distance metric?
analysis.context: K-means is a popular partitioning clustering algorithm but performs poorly due to outliers and the choice of distance metric. Existing methods either completely remove outlier data points from the clustering process or fail to account for data skewness when updating centroids.
methods: Normalization of multivariate dataset attributes into positive values between 1 and 90 to prevent division by zero
A new distance metric combining ratio proportionality, arctangent-based angles, and root mean square error (RMSE)
An adapted Tukey's rule that divides the constant into r1 and r2 depending on data distribution skewness (left, right, or balanced relative to the mean)
A modified k-means algorithm where outlier removal via the adapted Tukey's rule is applied recursively per attribute during centroid updating rather than deleting entire data points
Validation and performance comparison across nine standard multivariate UCI datasets measuring purity, iteration count, and runtime
main_findings: The modified k-means algorithm improved overall clustering accuracy up to 80.57% across nine standard multivariate datasets, outperforming conventional k-means, k-means#, and several evolutionary algorithms
The adapted Tukey's rule reduced the overall iteration number for centroid convergence by approximately 50% compared to the standard Tukey's rule
The proposed distance metric outperformed standard Euclidean, cosine, and correlation metrics by 2.40%, 5.79%, and 6.15% in overall clustering accuracy respectively
Recursive attribute-wise outlier removal successfully prevented the creation of empty clusters that typically occur when entire outlier data points containing multiple attributes are dropped
assumptions: Real-world data is not always ideal and may contain noisy observations or outliers generated by abnormal phenomena
Data skewness can be detected and managed by counting data points on the left and right sides of the mean value
Clustering accuracy is considered a primary objective in critical applications regardless of additional computational time
limitations_explicit: The outlier removal step adds extra processing time to the procedure of the conventional k-means, making the adapted Tukey's rule worse in processing run-time
The proposed distance metric is limited to real values greater than zero, requiring additional processing time for data normalization
Data clustering with a high variety of possible clusters (such as in the Blood dataset) degrades the clustering accuracy of the modified k-means

potential_open_questions.question: How can the time complexity and run-time overhead introduced by the recursive adapted Tukey's rule be reduced for big data clustering applications?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: The current recursive outlier removal and adaptation steps increase computational processing time compared to standard k-means, which limits its suitability for real-time or massive datasets without further runtime optimization.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The paper notes that the adapted Tukey's rule increases processing time and explicitly identifies improving run-time for big data clustering as future work.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: In this manuscript, several modifications are proposed for the k-means algorithm based on the adapted Tukey's rule for outliers removal and the new distance metric. Although the significant improvement in clustering accuracy, several challenges face the modified k-means such as real-time clustering due to the outliers removal step that added extra processing time to the procedure of the conventional k-means. Also, the proposed distance metric is limited to real values greater than zero. This needs additional processing time for data normalization. However, the biding between the clustering accuracy and run-time highly depends on the application filed. On the other hand, data clustering with high variety number of possible clusters such as in Blood dataset is another challenge to the proposed algorithm. This variety in number of clusters degrades the clustering accuracy using the modified k-means.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Applying the adapted Tukey's rule and the new distance metric to alternative partitioning algorithms such as fuzzy c-means and k-medoids will similarly improve their clustering accuracy and centroid convergence.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Since the proposed adapted Tukey's rule and distance metric successfully address centroid distortion and similarity measurement in standard k-means, their core mechanisms for handling skewness and outlier mitigation can generalize to other center-based clustering algorithms.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The authors explicitly propose applying these components to fuzzy c-means and k-medoids as a direction for future research.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: On the other hand, the developed distance metric properly aided the modified k-means in term of the overall accuracy performance compared to the other distance metrics. Generally, the proposed distance metric outperformed the Euclidean, cosine and correlation metrics by 2.40%, 5.79% and 6.15% of the clustering accuracy, respectively. In future work, the adapted Tukey’s rule and the new distance metric will be applied to various clustering algorithms such as fuzzy c-means and k-medoids. Moreover, improving the run-time of modified k-means for big data clustering will be investigated further in future work by reducing the time complexity of Tukey’s rule for outlier removal.

analysis.paper_title: Outlier Detection Method based on Improved K-means Clustering Algorithm
analysis.authors_year: Wenfen Liu, Nan Wang, Yuehua Huang, 2021
analysis.research_question: How can the K-means clustering algorithm be modified to prevent edge points and outliers from misleading the clustering process and centroid updates while effectively detecting outliers?
analysis.context: Traditional K-means clustering is sensitive to outliers and edge points, which can mislead centroid updates and degrade clustering and outlier detection performance. This paper proposes an improved K-means clustering and outlier detection method designed to maintain traditional K-means ease of implementation and high efficiency while performing well on low-dimensional convex data sets.
methods: Adaptive edge point detection in clusters using local standard deviation thresholds derived from the distance distribution of data points to the centroid
Exclusion of edge points during centroid updates in each clustering iteration

Iterative post-clustering outlier detection where the farthest point in each cluster is successively placed into an outlier cluster until cluster average distance stabilizes or reaches maximum iterations
Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) for high-dimensional public data sets
Comparative evaluations against LOF, COPOD, and K-means# using artificial and public data sets from the ODDS website measured by AUC, accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score
main_findings: Ignoring edge points during centroid updates helps find centroids more quickly and accelerates convergence.
Performing outlier detection after clustering is completed improves the accuracy of outlier identification.

The proposed method (K-means*) achieves competitive or superior performance compared to baseline algorithms such as LOF, COPOD, and K-means# on both artificial and public data sets, demonstrating stability and effectiveness.
assumptions: The data contains normal clusters that are more concentrated and abnormal clusters or outliers that are more sparse.
The number of clusters k can be provided in advance or estimated using rules like the elbow rule.
Low-dimensional convex data sets exhibit characteristics suitable for centroid-based clustering extensions.
limitations_explicit: The K-means clustering algorithm needs to set the value of k (the number of clusters) in advance.
For high-dimensional ODDS data sets, dimensionality reduction via PCA is necessary to avoid adverse effects on experimental outcomes.

analysis.paper_title: K-means clustering algorithms: A comprehensive review, variants analysis, and advances in the era of big data
analysis.research_question: What are the existing variants of K-means algorithms for solving clustering problems since its inception to date?
analysis.context: The paper presents a comprehensive review, taxonomy, and analysis of the K-means clustering algorithm and its variants, discussing current trends, open issues, challenges, and future research directions in the era of big data.
methods: Systematic literature review following Kitchenham et al. guidelines
Electronic search across six major academic databases (ACM Digital Library, Elsevier Journal Access, Wiley Online Library, IEEE Xplore, Springer, Taylor & Francis)
Screening of retrieved articles using inclusion and exclusion criteria
Taxonomical classification of K-means variants into design variants and implementation variants
main_findings: K-means variants span algorithm input, algorithm processes, algorithmic output, and general concept modifications.
Implementation-level enhancements include parallel machine implementations, quantum machine implementations, and MapReduce framework adaptations.
A major portion of research has focused on solving initialization and centroid selection problems.
Outlier sensitivity, high data dimensionality, and automatic determination of cluster number remain significant open challenges.
assumptions: Standard K-means assumes spherical or ball-shaped clusters due to the Euclidean distance metric.
Real-world data collected in large quantities often follow a Gaussian distribution.
limitations_explicit: Standard K-means requires the number of clusters k to be specified a priori.
The standard algorithm is sensitive to initial centroid selection and outliers.
Standard K-means can struggle to discover non-spherical or overlapping cluster shapes.

potential_open_questions.question: How can an initialization technique for K-means be developed that is simple to implement, has low time complexity, and requires no additional parameters?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Despite numerous proposed techniques such as random selection, furthest point heuristics, sorting heuristics, density-based, projection-based, and splitting techniques, a clear state-of-the-art method that universally satisfies these conditions is still missing in the literature.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The paper highlights that despite many comparative studies on initialization methods, a definitive state-of-the-art technique is missing, leaving a need for simple, low-complexity initialization without extra parameters.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: Accurate determination of initial centroids from the given dataset is another aspect of the K-means initialization problem. According to Fränti and Sieranoja [66]; solving the problem of locating initial centroids is very difficult. Several techniques have been proposed in the literature addressing the issue of the K-means algorithm’s initial centroid selection. These include random selection, furthest point heuristic, sorting heuristic, density-based, projection-based, and splitting techniques. Several comparisons have been carried out and reported in the literature [169,83,204,36,107] in order to determine which of them is consistently better than others in terms of comparable computational requirements. Fränti and Sieranoja [66] reported that a clear state-of-the-art is missing. Therefore, there is a need for an initialization technique for K-means that is simple to implement with low time complexity and no additional parameters.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Incorporating an integrated outlier detection and removal scheme into the K-means algorithm will improve clustering stability and reduce the sum of squared errors within clusters.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: Outliers mislead classical K-means by disproportionately influencing mean calculations and increasing the within-cluster sum of squares, leading to unstable clusters across multiple runs.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The paper notes that outliers increase the sum of squared errors and cause unstable clusters across runs, suggesting that an integrated outlier detection and removal scheme is necessary to enhance performance.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: Sensitivity to outliers: A dataset with many outliers produces unstable clusters with several K-means clustering algorithm runs. The presence of outliers in the dataset also increases the sum of square error within clusters, thus affecting the accuracy of the final clustering result [193]. There is a need to incorporate an outlier detection and removal scheme into the K-means algorithm to improve its performance further.

analysis.paper_title: Optimal Approximation for Clustering with Outliers
analysis.authors_year: Akanksha Agrawal, Tanmay Inamdar, Saket Saurabh, and Jie Xue (2023)
analysis.research_question: How to design a general, approximation-preserving reduction from clustering with outliers problems (such as k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut) to their outlier-free counterparts to obtain optimal fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) approximation algorithms?
analysis.context: Real-world datasets often contain noise or outliers that can drastically distort clusters produced by standard algorithms. While clustering with outliers has been extensively studied, existing FPT approximation schemes either suffered from suboptimal approximation ratios or required problem-specific geometric properties. This paper introduces a unified framework that reduces outlier-trimming clustering problems to standard clustering problems in an approximation-preserving manner.
methods: Formulating a lower bound instance of (k+m)-Median (or (k+m, z)-clustering) by co-locating facilities with clients.
Computing a constant-factor approximate center set A using a polynomial-time oracle algorithm.
Partitioning points into concentric rings around each center in A based on geometric distance scales.
Constructing a weighted coreset S by uniformly sampling from large rings and assigning appropriate integer weights.
Proving a concentration bound (Lemma 1 and Lemma 4) to guarantee that the weighted sample preserves clustering cost even after excluding m outliers.
Enumerating all subsets T of size at most m from the coreset S and solving the resulting outlier-free weighted k-Median instances.
main_findings: A general FPT reduction framework that converts any β-approximation for standard k-Median into a (β + ϵ)-approximation for k-MedianOut with running time ((k + m)/ϵ)^{O(m)} · T(n, k) · n^{O(1)}.
Optimal FPT approximation ratios of (1 + 2/e + ϵ) for k-MedianOut and (1 + 8/e + ϵ) for k-MeansOut in general metrics.
Optimal (1 + ϵ)-approximation algorithms for k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut in special metric spaces such as constant doubling dimensions, graphs of bounded treewidth, and minor-free graphs.
Successful extension of the framework to constrained clustering variants including Matroid Median with Outliers, Colorful k-Median, and general (k, z)-clustering with outliers.
assumptions: The underlying metric space satisfies symmetry and the triangle inequality.
An efficient polynomial-time τ-approximation algorithm exists for the outlier-free (k+m)-median or (k+m, z)-clustering instance.
A β-approximation algorithm is available for the standard (weighted) k-median or k-clustering problem.
Weights assigned to sampled points in the coreset can be treated as integers or adjusted via separated subsets for small and large residue groups.
limitations_explicit: The FPT running time depends exponentially on the number of outliers m through a factor of ((k + m)/ϵ)^{O(m)}.
For metric spaces where squares of distances do not satisfy the triangle inequality (such as k-Means), specialized technical adjustments (relaxed triangle inequality) are required.

potential_open_questions.question: Is it possible to obtain approximation guarantees for k-MedianOut matching that for k-Median with a running time that is FPT in k and ϵ alone, avoiding the FPT dependence on the number of outliers m?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: Current reduction frameworks necessitate enumerating subsets of size up to m from the coreset, leading to an (O(m)) exponent in the running time bound that remains an open structural barrier.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The authors highlight that a fundamental open question is whether the FPT dependence on the number of outliers m is strictly necessary or if matching outlier-free running times depending only on k and ϵ are achievable.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt:
5. Concluding Remarks
In this paper, we give a reduction from k-MedianOut to k-Median that runs in time FPT in k, m, and ϵ, and preserves the approximation ratio up to an additive ϵ factor. As a consequence, we obtain improved FPT approximations for k-MedianOut in general as well as special kinds of metrics, and these approximation guarantees are known to be tight in general. Furthermore, our technique is versatile in that it also gives improved approximations for related clustering problems, such as k-MeansOut, Matroid Median with Outliers, and Colorful k-Median, among others.
The most natural direction is to improve the FPT running time while obtaining the tight approximation ratios. More fundamentally, perhaps, is the question whether we need an FPT dependence on the number of outliers, m; or whether it is possible to obtain approximation guarantees for k-MedianOut matching that for k-Median, with a running time that is FPT in k and ϵ alone.

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: For any clustering objective with a cost function defined by the z-th power of distances where z >= 1, sampling points via concentric ring partitions around a (k+m)-median approximate solution yields a coreset size bounded independently of the total point count n, preserving costs under optimal outlier removal.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: By generalizing concentration bounds using relaxed triangle inequalities for z-th powers, the approximation error between weighted samples and original rings remains bounded by ϵ times the optimal clustering cost.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The authors establish that the coreset construction and concentration lemmas generalize from k-MedianOut to arbitrary (k, z)-clustering with outliers by appropriately scaling parameters and invoking z-th power distance properties.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt:
4.1 k-Means with Outliers
This is similar to k-MedianOut, except that the cost function is the sum of squares of distances of all except m outlier points to a set of k facilities. This generalizes the well-known k-Means problem. Here, the main obstacle is that, the squares of distances do not satisfy triangle inequality, and thus it does not form a metric. However, they satisfy a relaxed version of triangle inequality (i.e., d(p, q)^2 ≤ 2(d(p, r)^2 + d(r, q)^2)). This technicality makes the arguments tedious, nevertheless, we can follow the same approach as for k-MedianOut, to obtain optimal FPT approximation schemes. Our technique implies an optimal (1 + 8/e + ϵ)-approximation for k-MeansOut (using the result of (Cohen-Addad et al., 2019) as a black-box), improving upon polynomial-time 53.002-approximation from (Krishnaswamy et al., 2018), and (9 + ϵ)-approximation from (Goyal et al., 2020) in time FPT in k, m and ϵ.
In fact, using our technique, we can get improved approximation guarantees for (k, z)-Clustering with Outliers, where the cost function involves z-th power of distances, where z ≥ 1 is fixed for a problem. Note that the cases z = 1 and z = 2 correspond to k-MedianOut and k-MeansOut respectively. We give the details for (k, z)-Clustering with Outliers in Appendix A.

analysis.paper_title: Transforming Complex Problems Into K-Means Solutions
analysis.authors_year: Hongfu Liu, Junxiang Chen, Jennifer Dy, and Yun Fu, 2023
analysis.research_question: How can available approaches in generalizing K-means be unified to solve challenging and complex non-standard cluster analysis problems across multiple domains?
analysis.context: The paper provides a survey and unifying framework for generalizing K-means clustering—traditionally focused on standard squared Euclidean distance—to address complex problems through transformations in data representation, distance measures, label assignments, and centroid updates.
methods: Generalizing K-means framework via four aspects: data input, distance measure, label assignment, and centroid updating
Mathematical reformulation of non-standard problems into modified K-means formulations
Iterative subspace projection and clustering via kernel K-means
Utility-based consensus clustering and spectral ensemble clustering via weighted K-means
Partition level constrained clustering and domain adaptation via concatenated matrix representations and incomplete centroid updating
Joint clustering and outlier detection (COR) via partition space transformation and K-means–
main_findings: Complex problems such as iterative subspace projection, consensus clustering, spectral ensemble clustering, constrained clustering, domain adaptation, and joint outlier detection can be elegantly solved by modified K-means algorithms with theoretical convergence guarantees.
Data transformations, such as one-hot encoding for binary matrices or concatenation with side information, bridge disparate problem domains into the K-means objective function structure.

Generalized K-means solutions match or exceed the effectiveness of competitive specialized methods while achieving significantly higher computational efficiency (e.g., reducing spectral clustering complexities from cubic/quadratic to linear time).
assumptions: Centroid updating rules must match the chosen K-means distance function to guarantee algorithmic convergence.
Auxiliary zeros or missing values in concatenated matrices or incomplete data should not contribute to centroid calculations or distance computations.
Prototypical assumptions and Euclidean-like formulations can be extended using alternative metrics or divergences such as Bregman divergences and Point-to-Centroid (P2C) distances.
limitations_explicit: Standard K-means fails to capture non-spherical cluster structures due to the prototypical assumption.
The sensitivity of K-means initialization heavily affects clustering performance.
The requirement of a pre-defined cluster number is a known drawback of K-means.

potential_open_questions.question: How can the pre-defined cluster number parameter in K-means frameworks be robustly selected or eliminated across diverse generalized problem domains without relying on external heuristics?
potential_open_questions.why_unresolved: While the paper surveys generalization strategies across distance, data input, label assignment, and centroid updating, it explicitly excludes further discussion regarding the selection of the pre-defined cluster number, noting that almost every clustering algorithm requires its own parameters.
potential_open_questions.evidence: The paper notes that pre-defined cluster numbers are a common drawback of clustering algorithms and leaves further discussion regarding its selection outside the scope of the review.
potential_open_questions.evidence_excerpt: It is also arguable that the pre-defined cluster number is another drawback of K-means. In fact, almost every clustering algorithm requires its own parameters, including K-means. However, further discussion regarding its selection is beyond the scope of this paper.
sections: D. Advantages and Limitations of K-Means

candidate_hypotheses.hypothesis: Transforming complex non-standard clustering and fusion tasks into modified K-means formulations with appropriate data transformations and distance functions preserves local convergence guarantees while drastically reducing computational complexity to linear time.
candidate_hypotheses.rationale: By rewriting objective functions from graph partitioning, consensus utility functions, and constrained optimization into matrix-wise Frobenius norm or K-means objectives, optimization can be performed efficiently via Lloyd's or Hartigan's algorithms.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence: The paper demonstrates theoretically and experimentally that reformulating problems like spectral ensemble clustering and constrained clustering into K-means frameworks reduces complexities from O(n^3) and O(n^2) to O(n) while maintaining convergence.
candidate_hypotheses.evidence_excerpt: By the above transformation, the time complexity of SEC is O(tnrK). Thus, the transformation dramatically reduces the time and space complexities from O(n3) and O(n2) of the standard spectral clustering on the co-association matrix, respectively, to O(n). Note that there is only one non-zero element in bl,i.
